title: Nutrient Cycles
hook: The carbon in your breath, the nitrogen in your DNA, the water in your blood — all of it has cycled through living things and the planet countless times. Nothing is used up; everything is recycled.
key_points: Matter is recycled through ecosystems in loops called biogeochemical cycles.
The carbon cycle moves carbon between air, living things, oceans, and rocks.
The nitrogen cycle relies on bacteria to make atmospheric nitrogen usable for life.
The water cycle moves water through evaporation, rain, rivers, and organisms.
content_html: Ecosystems run on two currencies: energy and matter. Energy flows through and is lost as heat, so it has to be resupplied constantly by the sun. Matter is different — it's recycled. The same atoms of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen are used again and again, passing from air to plant to animal to soil and back. Ecologists call these loops biogeochemical cycles, and they're what keep finite supplies of vital elements perpetually in circulation.
extra_html: Take three of the big ones, as Khan Academy lays them out. In the carbon cycle, plants pull carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis, animals eat the plants, and respiration and decay release the carbon back — with some locked away for ages in oceans and rock. The nitrogen cycle has a twist: nitrogen gas makes up most of the air, but living things can't use it directly, so specialized bacteria "fix" it into usable compounds, making them quiet linchpins of nearly all life. The water cycle drives evaporation, rainfall, and the flow of rivers, and threads through every organism that drinks or transpires. These cycles interlock, and disrupting one — say, by burning fossil carbon faster than it can be reabsorbed — ripples through the rest.

related.title: Ecosystems & Interdependence
related.hook: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus their environment, all so tangled together that pulling one thread can shake the whole web.

related.title: Food Chains & Energy Flow
related.hook: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, gets captured by plants, and flows up the menu — but it leaks away at every bite, so the chain stays short.

flashcards.prompt: Unlike energy, which flows through and leaves an ecosystem, what happens to matter like carbon and nitrogen?

choices.text: It is recycled, cycling repeatedly through living and non-living parts
It is destroyed and must be created anew each year
It escapes into space and never returns

flashcards.explanation_html: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat, but matter cycles. Atoms of carbon, nitrogen, and water are used over and over in biogeochemical cycles.

flashcards.prompt: Plants can't use nitrogen straight from the air. What makes atmospheric nitrogen usable for life?

choices.text: Bacteria that 'fix' nitrogen into compounds plants can absorb
Sunlight breaking nitrogen apart in leaves
Plants inhaling nitrogen gas through their roots

flashcards.explanation_html: Most life can't use inert nitrogen gas (N₂). Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert it into forms like ammonia that plants can take up — a critical step in the cycle.

flashcards.prompt: Name three major nutrient cycles that move matter through ecosystems.
flashcards.back_html: The carbon cycle, the nitrogen cycle, and the water cycle — each moving a key substance between the atmosphere, living things, and the Earth.
